title: Apprenticeship and skills: the unfinished promise
author: Editorial Desk
summary: Training schemes need quality, stipend and a job at the end.
body:
India has a young population and a large gap between the skills that young people have and the skills that employers look for. Several programmes exist to close that gap: apprenticeship under the Apprentices Act, 1961, the Skill India programmes, the National Skill Development Corporation (NSDC) and the Industrial Training Institutes (ITIs). Yet many young people finish a course and still cannot find work. This post looks at how apprenticeship is meant to work, what the law and the main scheme provide, where the promise falls short, and what BMS asks for.

## What an apprentice is

An apprentice is not an ordinary employee. An apprenticeship is a contract under which a person learns a trade or occupation on the job, in a real establishment, for a fixed period, and receives a stipend. The Apprentices Act, 1961, allows employers to use their facilities for practical training in order to build a pool of skilled workers. The Act has been amended several times, in 1973, 1986 and 2014, to widen its scope. The 2014 amendment brought in non-engineering fields and allowed employers to design "optional trades" with their own syllabi, and it allowed more than one employer to share training.

## How the system is organised

The Directorate General of Training, under the Ministry of Skill Development and Entrepreneurship, oversees trade apprentices in central undertakings and in establishments operating in four or more States, through regional directorates. State Apprenticeship Advisers oversee trade apprentices in State government undertakings and private establishments. A tripartite statutory body, the Central Apprenticeship Council, advises the Government on policy and standards. The categories of apprentice include trade, graduate, technician, technician (vocational) and optional trade apprentices.

The minimum age for an apprentice is 14, and 18 for designated trades in hazardous industries. Training lasts one year for ITI pass-outs and two years for freshers in designated trades, and six, nine or twelve months in optional trades.

## What the law says about numbers and stipend

Employers with 40 or more workers, and the required training facilities, are expected to engage apprentices equal to 2.5 to 10 per cent of their total manpower, including contract staff. For trade apprentices, the minimum stipend is a share of the State's semi-skilled minimum wage: 70 per cent in the first year, 80 per cent in the second, and 90 per cent in the third and fourth years. For graduate, technician and technician (vocational) apprentices, minimum monthly stipends of Rs 4,984, Rs 3,542 and Rs 2,758 were fixed from December 2014, with the cost shared equally by the employer and the Centre.

Two further points are important for young people. First, the employer is not bound to offer a job after training: recruitment of completed apprentices is at the employer's discretion. Second, laws such as those on provident fund, state insurance, minimum wages and industrial disputes do not apply to apprentices, because they are trainees and not employees. This is why a fair stipend and a reliable certificate matter so much.

## The national scheme to encourage employers

The National Apprenticeship Promotion Scheme (NAPS-2) is the Government's tool to make apprenticeship attractive to employers. It partly funds the stipend: the Government pays 25 per cent of the stipend, up to Rs 1,500 per apprentice per month, directly to the apprentice's bank account. The scheme excludes central and State government departments, public sector undertakings and public sector banks, and large private organisations are encouraged to forgo the support. It specifically encourages enrolment in micro, small and medium enterprises and in less-served areas such as aspirational districts and the North-East. For support, the upper age at registration is 35.

## What works

Whatever the scheme, the experience of employers and trainees points to a few things that work:

- Apprenticeships with real work in real firms, where the trainee does tasks that are part of production and is supervised.
- Courses linked to the demand of local industry, so that the skill taught is the skill that is wanted nearby.
- A stipend that allows poorer youths to take part, since a trainee who cannot afford the bus fare cannot attend.
- Recognised certificates that employers trust, so that training in one firm is portable to another.

## What does not

- Courses that end with a certificate but no placement.
- Outdated equipment and syllabi in training institutes.
- Low-quality private training providers who collect fees and teach little.
- Using apprentices as cheap labour, with no systematic learning, to fill jobs that should be regular posts.

The last point deserves attention. The law's fair purpose is to train, and a firm that replaces regular workers with a rolling set of apprentices defeats it.

## The link with employment incentives

Skilling is closely tied to the Government's employment policy. The Employment Linked Incentive (ELI) scheme, approved in July 2025 with an outlay of Rs 99,446 crore, aims to support more than 3.5 crore jobs over two years, including about 1.92 crore first-time employees. A first-time worker registered with the EPFO can receive one month's EPF wage, up to Rs 15,000, in two instalments, and employers who add jobs are also given incentives. Such schemes work best when young people are trained to take up the jobs created, and that is where apprenticeship and skilling meet employment.

## What BMS asks for

BMS has asked that skill programmes be tied to employment, that apprentices be paid fairly, and that micro and small enterprises, which are major employers, be supported to take apprentices, since they often lack the capacity to run training on their own. BMS has welcomed measures that link incentives with first-time employment, as with the ELI scheme, and has also asked for attention to labour-intensive sectors such as beedi, handlooms, agriculture and fisheries in its memorandum to the Labour Minister. The thought behind these demands is that skill is a form of national capital: investing in the worker's ability pays back to the enterprise and to the country many times over, a view that fits BMS's emphasis on the worker as a builder of the nation.

## What remains to be done

- **Placement tracking:** a public record of how many trained persons actually find work, by course and by institute.
- **Stipend discipline:** regular payment through the bank, and fair treatment so that apprentices are not used as substitutes for regular staff.
- **Support to small firms:** simple procedures, shared training facilities and clear reimbursement so that MSMEs can take apprentices.
- **Quality control:** upgrading equipment in ITIs and holding private providers to standards.
- **Guidance for youth:** easy information about which trades have openings in their district.

## A closing word

The promise of skilling is simple: that a young person who learns a trade will find work in it, and be paid fairly. It remains unfinished wherever training and employment run on separate tracks. The measures that join them, real apprenticeships, fair stipends, support for small employers and honest placement records, are the ones that turn a certificate into a livelihood.
